Senses.Note: Pinjixiang Zhixiang raises Yunmen's complete two-light-diseases saying, then asks how apparent clarity can still conceal an object. The quoted line is Yunmen's; Pinjixiang makes the present analytical test. Tianqi Benrui reproduces Yunmen's two-light-diseases passage in his case notes, then adds his own marked summative verse about obstructed vision and a lone boat. Yunmen speaks the headword; Tianqi supplies a separate current interpretation. These are two independent present uses; evidence depth remains provisional. Tianyin Yuanxiu points his staff at a lamp and asks whether naming it a lamp is either adequate or a mistake. Senses.PreferredTarget: When light and its objects are both forgotten, what is this?
AlternateTargets: If illumination and its field are both forgotten, what remains to be named?
SearchAliases: Panshan light objects forgotten what is this
light and field both forgotten Chan question
Senses.Note: Panshan's verse first says that light does not illuminate an object and the object does not remain; this question presses further when both are forgotten. Miyun contrasts it with Dongshan's opposite question, Feiyin challenges both, Baiyu overturns the verse with a staff, and Miyin applies it to a lay disciple's response. Their comments make the exact question a test of what one can say or do at this point, beyond an account of light and object.

SearchAliases: at the gate of light and shadow
Zen at the gate of light and shadow
Senses.Explanation: The gate of light and shadow is the records' visible threshold contrasted with the matter inside the house: people mistake its coarse, shallow business for what is within (光影門頭戶底麤淺底事，將作屋裏事). Elsewhere Xueguan Zhiyin says students "recognize only the gate of light and shadow as themselves" (惟認光影門頭當作自己). The phrase also enters verse as a place not to stop: "do not halt your steps at the gate of light and shadow" (光影門頭休駐足). Hongzhi supplies a notable counter-use: "a person who settles the matter at the gate of light and shadow will do" (光影門頭了事底漢即得), then immediately asks how one proceeds before guest and host divide and before an image is formed. Zen thus bends ordinary light, shadow, and doorway language into a recurring label for the visible or reflected threshold that records contrast with the inside of the house, oneself, and the not-yet-formed image.

Entries.SourceTerm: 光明寂照遍河沙，凡聖含靈共我家

Senses.PreferredTarget: Luminous stillness shines across the sands of the Ganges; sages and ordinary beings belong to my home
AlternateTargets: Light silently illumines the Ganges sands, and all beings are of one household
SearchAliases: luminous stillness Ganges sands all beings one home
Zhang Zhuo light shines Ganges saints ordinary people
Senses.Note: Zhang Zhuo, a lay scholar, speaks the complete eight-line verse after his encounter with Shishuang; this pair opens it. Sanyi explains the line against a shallow claim of luminous awareness, Xueguan challenges the verse as still short of a further turn, Binya both praises and tests it, Eryin rewrites its opening into a new verse, and Baiyu answers its richness with a poem of poverty. The exact opening words remain Zhang Zhuo's; the later masters have separate current deployments.

Entries.SourceTerm: 光未發時，汝等諸人向甚麼處委

Senses.PreferredTarget: Before the light appeared, where would you have placed yourselves?
AlternateTargets: Before the light shone, where could you locate yourselves?
SearchAliases: Before the light shone, where could you locate yourselves?
Senses.Note: An old question about wisdom-light asks where anyone could stand before its appearance. Miyin invokes it while instructing a lay disciple; Wansong uses Changsha Jingcen's version in an active reading of an old case.

Occurrences.Kwic: 來，將去瞞神蓋鬼，吐向無眼人前，不辨來風，方道祖師門下不過如斯也。遇著明眼作家，輕輕挑動，猶如醬缸蟲子相似。所以教中道：「如聾奏音樂，悅彼不自聞，於法不修行，多聞亦如是。」上根之人見月忘指，中下之人依語作務。凡看佛教覽群書者，先明其本，然後則有少分相應也。示省凡羅居士示省凡羅居士直心向道，不假佗力，須要當人有大信根。但於二六時中裏，行住坐臥處，時時返照、切切提撕，看是甚麼道理，豁向一毛端頭覷得徹去。在聖位中亦如是，凡夫地中也亦然。所以道：「三世諸佛共法界眾生，盡是摩訶般若光。光未發時，汝等諸人向甚麼處委？」到這裏，有心莫能測，有語莫能宣，正宣雖不得，觸著又現前，管取一動一靜，便與先佛世尊圜一受用也。示越為禪人示越為禪人徹明此事，非在捨鬧而趣靜，背境以觀心。若作如是見解，則成大病也。舉世莫能醫，但看觸境逢緣，覿面放過，當知落在第二義邊。驀直拈來，舉向山僧，無藥對治，定然一棒打折你腰，教你伸也不可得，縮也不可得，痛也不可得，癢也不可得，病然出體，絲點無存，通身暢快，本不相干。設若未能，又成毛病矣。毛病既不除，一味業識茫茫，無本可據，專在意識裏卜度，情解中思想，朝吟暮詠，不生厭繁
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J35/J35nB343.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Miyin of Shengjue Monastery, Guangfu Mountain. Occurrences.Kwic: 云：和尚莫謾人好。福云：却是你謾我。若喚作銅鐵聲，情封則物；聲不是聲，理契則神。所以三藏、玄沙瞻前不能顧後。為甚保福見僧道：和尚莫謾人好。保福道：却是你謾我。誣人之罪，以罪加之。第六十五則長沙轉物第六十五則長沙轉物舉：僧問長沙：作麼生轉得山河大地歸自己去？沙云：作麼生轉自己歸山河大地去？天童拈云：雖然主賓互喚，要且泥水不分，忽然捩轉鼻孔，恁麼不恁麼總不得，又合作麼生？如今王令稍嚴，不許人攙行奪市。師云：湖南長沙招賢大師上堂云：我常向汝諸人道：三世諸佛共盡法界眾生是摩訶般若光。光未發時，汝等諸人向甚麼處委？光未發時，尚無佛無眾生消息，何處得山河國土來？萬松嘗道：混沌未分時，還有天地人不？父母未生時，還有己身不？心念未起時，還有迷悟凡聖不？這僧尚問：如何轉得山河大地歸自己去？一大藏教祇說箇三界唯心，萬法唯識。肇法師云：會萬物為自己者，其唯聖人乎？楞嚴經道：若能轉物，即同如來。白雲端頌云：若能轉物即如來，春暖山花處處開。自有一雙窮相手，不曾容易舞三臺。所以天童道：不許人攙行奪市。此轉物話，忝解教乘者亦皆知有，而飽參衲子却不得受用。所以長沙却與倒過道：如何轉得自己歸山河大地去？天童
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X67/X67n1307.xml). Elder Wansong’s Commentary and Chanted Remarks on Master Tiantong Jue’s Picking Up Ancient Cases: Record of Requests for Instruction. In his commentary on an old Changsha exchange about turning mountains and earth toward oneself, Wansong explicitly quotes Changsha Jingcen asking where Buddhas and beings could be before wisdom-light appeared. Wansong then poses parallel questions about the world before division and thought before it arises, and returns to the monk's attempt to turn the world. Changsha is the named speaker of the selected question; Wansong makes it a present test of the case.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：「如何是天得一以清？」師云：「雲散家家月。」「如何是地得一以寧？」師云：「春來樹樹花。」「如何是君王得一以治平？」師云：「位臨南面。」進云：「和尚得一又如何？」師云：「倒著袈裟閒拍掌。」進云：「未審年朝祝聖一句作麼生道？」師云：「一人有慶，兆民賴之。」進云：「恁麼則金枝永茂三千界，玉葉常敷萬古春。」師云：「且喜闍黎得話會。」乃云：「舊年離未遠，新歲恰三朝，新舊不相參，世相得常住。所以道：旋嵐偃嶽而常靜，江河競注而不流，野馬飄鼓而不動，日月歷天而不周。花根本豔，虎體原斑，雖然不改舊時顏，未免人人添一歲。大眾！新舊且置，如何是世相得常住？」卓拄杖，云：「千古長如白練飛，一條界破青山色。」施主請上堂。「繁興大用，舉必全真，不審低聲，無非了義。因機有異，法有差殊，半滿偏圓，悉皆平等。故曰：『佛以一音演說法，眾生隨類各得解。』是以維摩大士以一缽飽三萬二千菩薩。只如甘贄行者設粥南泉，打破粥鍋，且道是繁興大用？不是繁興大用？」豎拂，云：「等閒識得東風面，萬紫千紅總是春。」西林菴，上堂。「夏日初臨四月天，村庄那個得安閒？衲僧分上無餘事，秪要知歸便放參。莫有知歸者麼？」良久，云：「自是不歸歸便得，五湖煙景有誰爭？」接濟菴，上堂。「遶菴溪水深千尺，四裏村庄得萬家，饑餐渴飲前朝事，亙古流香掛齒牙。」復云：「昨日正法來，今朝留接濟，菴寺雖有殊，主人原不異。要明不異主，春風吹柳絮，於此豁雙眸，洞明第一義。還知第一義麼？日高花影重，風暖鳥聲碎。」上堂。「佛佛授手無別授，祖祖相傳無別傳，炎蒸六月如臨火，誰不通身汗似泉？說到行不到，鐘中無鼓響；行到說不到，鼓中無鐘聲；行說俱到，鐘鼓得交參。句句無先後，行說俱不到，用盡自己心，笑破他人口。且道離卻四句又作麼生？」喝一喝，云：「大抵還他肌骨好，不搽紅粉也風流。」上堂。「無相謂法身，無見謂法眼。以無相故，隨機現形；以無見故，隨照鑑物。了無造作，不假安排，亦名天真。佛性向上，玄機於中，聖凡不立，人我本空。世法、佛法，融成一片；情與無情，混作一團。自然上無攀仰、下絕己躬，髑髏常干世界，鼻孔摩觸家風，便能一為無量、無量為一，於一毫端現寶王剎，坐微塵裡轉大法輪。且道是什麼人得恁麼地？還委悉麼？披簑側立千峰外，引水澆蔬五老前。」蘇州府吳江報恩禪寺語錄蘇州府吳江報恩禪寺語錄

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB185.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Fushi. Fushi Tongxian applies Zhu Xi's spring lines after describing varied means of teaching as all belonging to complete activity. He quotes the Buddha speaking in one voice while beings understand differently, then sets Vimalakirti's one bowl feeding many bodhisattvas beside Nanquan breaking a porridge pot. Are both great activity or not? He raises his whisk and answers with recognizing the east wind through all the purple and red of spring. One spring appearing in diverse flowers supplies the image for this question about differing acts; it does not make the acts literally identical or describe a sudden change of weather in the hall. The headword is rendered: One readily recognizes the face of the east wind; every purple and red blossom is spring

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB187.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Tian’an Sheng. In Tian'an Sheng's exchange, an unnamed monk asks whether the spring garden's blossoming is Buddha teaching or worldly business. Asked further about swallows and orioles, Tian'an says every home's doorway has Guanyin. The monk then recites Zhu Xi's spring pair. Tian'an replies, 'Zhu Wen Gong has arrived,' explicitly recognizing the literary author being quoted. He goes on to scrutinize inherited formulas about the buddhas and future students and ends with the cock announcing the bell and people sitting in the spring breeze. Recognizing the poet is not a recorded declaration that the monk has attained the understanding he claims. The headword is rendered: One readily recognizes the face of the east wind; every purple and red blossom is spring

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J36/J36nB359.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Baiyu. Baiyu Jingsi quotes the complete four-line poem on New Year's Day. He first claims that although the buddhas and patriarchs have said innumerable things, nobody has yet said the new year's teaching, and promises to pour out his whole account for the assembly. Raising his whisk, he recites seeking fragrance on a fine day beside the Si River, the boundless scene newly renewed, and the closing east-wind pair. He then looks around and allows the listeners to criticize as they will. The inherited poem is made his present offering under a claim of a new occasion, with its adequacy expressly open to the assembly's assessment. The headword is rendered: One readily recognizes the face of the east wind; every purple and red blossom is spring

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J40/J40nB477.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Tianyixiang. Tianyi Juxiang imagines a different way of handling students: a cough can be called a lion's roar, a turn of the head an elephant's movement, and even stillness or silence can receive a favorable phrase. He lets listeners either trust him and undertake directly or refuse to be fooled, then quotes the spring pair. Immediately afterward he says this is still empty talk of mystery and requires proof face to face. He grabs the attendant and demands a line outside speech, silence, movement and stillness; the attendant cannot answer. The literary image is therefore followed by an actual test, not treated as an all-purpose certificate that every response already succeeds. The headword is rendered: One readily recognizes the face of the east wind; every purple and red blossom is spring

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J40/J40nB490.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Suruhan of Boshan. Suru Honghan places the pair in his reply to an imagined objector during a New Year address. His address reports a voice celebrating renewal and the flourishing of the household's teaching; his own response says there need be no further instructions if everything is carried out as stated. The objector complains that the teaching seat should release bonds rather than circulate worldly celebrations. Suru answers with the east-wind lines. One spring visible through diverse flowers answers that attempted division in this specific ceremonial setting. The words remain a quotation of Zhu Xi's poem within Suru's authored reply, not words composed by the hypothetical objector. The headword is rendered: One readily recognizes the face of the east wind; every purple and red blossom is spring

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB185.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Fushi. Fushi Tongxian applies Zhu Xi's spring lines after describing varied means of teaching as all belonging to complete activity. He quotes the Buddha speaking in one voice while beings understand differently, then sets Vimalakirti's one bowl feeding many bodhisattvas beside Nanquan breaking a porridge pot. Are both great activity or not? He raises his whisk and answers with recognizing the east wind through all the purple and red of spring. One spring appearing in diverse flowers supplies the image for this question about differing acts; it does not make the acts literally identical or describe a sudden change of weather in the hall. The headword is rendered: One readily recognizes the face of the east wind; every purple and red blossom is spring

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB187.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Tian’an Sheng. In Tian'an Sheng's exchange, an unnamed monk asks whether the spring garden's blossoming is Buddha teaching or worldly business. Asked further about swallows and orioles, Tian'an says every home's doorway has Guanyin. The monk then recites Zhu Xi's spring pair. Tian'an replies, 'Zhu Wen Gong has arrived,' explicitly recognizing the literary author being quoted. He goes on to scrutinize inherited formulas about the buddhas and future students and ends with the cock announcing the bell and people sitting in the spring breeze. Recognizing the poet is not a recorded declaration that the monk has attained the understanding he claims. ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J40/J40nB477.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Tianyixiang. Tianyi Juxiang imagines a different way of handling students: a cough can be called a lion's roar, a turn of the head an elephant's movement, and even stillness or silence can receive a favorable phrase. He lets listeners either trust him and undertake directly or refuse to be fooled, then quotes the spring pair. Immediately afterward he says this is still empty talk of mystery and requires proof face to face. He grabs the attendant and demands a line outside speech, silence, movement and stillness; the attendant cannot answer. The literary image is therefore followed by an actual test, not treated as an all-purpose certificate that every response already succeeds. Senses.Explanation: Grass bends as the wind passes: in these Chan addresses, an effective word or movement calls forth a response that follows its force. Yuanwu Keqin says that, once the grass bends with the moving wind, one cannot avoid following the waves. Gulin Qingmao uses the image for bringing many differences into line. Yinyuan Longqi says a single utterance can make the grass bend, extending a New Year address from a ruler's word to the assembly. Minshu Ruxiang places it in the lowered half of a staff formula and asks how that action is carried out. Yuanjie Jingying puts it beside freedom to respond to the occasion, then presses beyond fixed categories. Zhufeng Zhenxu pairs raising that turns heaven and earth with lowering that bends grass. Wanru Tongwei uses the image for the force of an upright command before which even a thousand sages cannot approach.

Senses.Explanation: “The grass bandit is decisively defeated” is a taunting verdict in an encounter. Zhaozhou Congshen says it after the hermitage owner ignores his movements; an unnamed monk says it during an exchange with Linji Yixuan; and Xinghua Cunjiang says it after Linji reviews their handling of a newcomer. Occurrences.Kwic: 德山背却法堂。著草鞋便行
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T48/T48n2003.xml). Blue Cliff Record by Chan Master Yuanwu Foguo. The Blue Cliff Record retells the encounter in which Deshan enters Guishan's hall, crosses it, looks around, and leaves. He returns, raises his sitting cloth, shouts at Guishan, and departs again; after turning his back on the hall he puts on straw sandals and walks away. Later Guishan tells the head monk that this visitor will one day build a hermitage and scold the Buddhas and ancestors. The selected words describe Deshan's physical departure in the case narrative. They are narrated by the record, not spoken by Deshan, and the surrounding comments evaluate the encounter rather than redefining the footwear.

ActorAttribution.GrammarEvidence: The exact clause narrates Deshan's action.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T48/T48n2005.xml). The Gateless Barrier. In the Gateless Barrier's cat case, Nansen threatens to cut a cat unless the assembly can say a saving word, and no one answers. Zhaozhou returns later, hears the event, puts a sandal on his head, and walks out; Nansen says that his presence would have saved the cat. Wumen Huikai then asks what Zhaozhou meant by carrying a straw sandal on his head, challenging readers to supply a fitting response. The headword is Wumen's own question about Zhaozhou's action, not a word that Zhaozhou says in the old case.

Occurrences.Kwic: 祖師玄旨是破草鞋。寧可赤脚不著最好。僧問。如何是佛。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X80/X80n1565.xml). Five Lamps Compendium. In Jiashan Shanhui's recorded instruction, he says that seeing one's nature leaves no Buddha to cling to and realizing the way leaves no teacher to retain. He calls the whole canon his sitting cloth and compares the patriarchs' profound purport to worn-out straw sandals; he adds that going barefoot would be better than wearing them. Senses.Explanation: Sandal money is the expense of travelling on foot in straw sandals. In the Huangbo–Nanquan exchange, Nanquan sets gruel-water money aside and asks who will repay the sandal money; later records say a reply saves sandal money or warn against wasting it. Senses.Explanation: ‘The leaf falls back to its root; it had no mouth when it came’ is Huineng's answer when disciples ask when he will return after leaving for Xinzhou. Later masters bring the pair into funerals, lineage verse and pointed questions about what coming and going mean. Chaozong Tongren quotes Huineng and Fayun Xiu at a Nirvana-day hall address, then says the no-mouth line means not coming and the no-nose line means not going. Juelang Daosheng puts the paired words in a lineage verse and calls the last barrier one that even a thousand sages cannot fathom. Shiqi Tongyun says the pair while a deceased master's bier is raised, then adds an impossible wooden-horse and mud-ox image. Yinyuan Longqi asks the assembly what can be said of the pair after praising an elder's work, and a monk answers with an iron snake across the old road. Yezhu Fuhui quotes the original Huineng exchange and two later masters' comments, then says all their case handling has exhausted itself and gives his own playful response. Chisong Daoling quotes the pair at a memorial for a patron's mother and substitutes a line about a fallen leaf becoming fruit and life continuing.

Senses.Note: Across the collected corpus the expression has 1,552 exact occurrences in 230 distinct works. The verb marks a failure to meet what is immediately at issue: hesitation, pursuit through words, a claim of understanding, or an unrecognized response can each constitute the miss. These are circumstances of one act, not separate senses. Three independent Tier-1/2 uses establish the sense; one compact lamp encounter is retained for its direct question-and-verdict form.

ClaimAnchors.ClaimText: 如何是此事
ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 麻谷便問。眨上眉毛即不問。如何是此事。師曰。蹉過也。谷乃掀倒禪牀。師便打。
ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Five Lamps Compendium (五燈會元). Magu Baoche asks what the matter is; Sanjiao Zongyin answers with the anchored verdict.

Senses.Explanation: 蹉過 means to miss it: to let what is immediately at issue pass without meeting it. In an authored instruction, Yuanwu Keqin says that once someone tries to pursue and capture the wordless matter, that person has already missed it; in a hall address he places the miss within the instant of raising an eyebrow. Dahui Zonggao tells a monk that he has missed it without knowing, making the word a verdict rather than a description of physical lateness; commenting on a Nanyang Huizhong case, he says that opening the eyes misses it and closing the eyes misses it too, then applies the verdict to his own wording. Baichi Xingyuan contrasts what remains plainly exact even when it cannot be counted with people who merely say ‘I understand’ and casually miss it. A lamp preserves Magu Baoche setting aside Sanjiao Zongyin's eyebrow warning and asking what the matter is; Sanjiao answers, ‘Missed it.’ Across these uses, hesitation, conceptual pursuit, unrecognized response, asserted understanding, and either side of an apparent alternative can all be the occasion of the same failure to meet what is present.

Senses.Explanation: “You have already missed it” is a direct verdict on a response, intention, gesture, or request. It appears after thanks are offered, when intention starts, and after a stock phrase is presented. Entries.SourceTerm: 轉山河大地歸自己則易，轉自己歸山河大地則難

Senses.PreferredTarget: Turning mountains and rivers into yourself is easy; turning yourself into them is hard
AlternateTargets: It is easy to bring the world into oneself, hard to return oneself to the world
SearchAliases: turning mountains and rivers into yourself is easy turning yourself into them is hard
Senses.Note: Dahui Zonggao contrasts taking mountains, rivers, and earth into oneself with giving oneself back to that world. Later masters question whether either act can be grasped as a technique: Jiqi and Wuzhun challenge the easy and difficult labels, Xueyan presses a disciple beyond them, and Yongjue rejects a self centered reading of the whole contrast.

Senses.Explanation: "Turning mountains and rivers into yourself is easy; turning yourself into them is hard" reverses the direction of a claim about self and world. Jiqi and Wuzhun challenge the pair by asking what can still be called self, world, or a move between them. Xueyan presses a disciple beyond the easy and hard labels; Yongjue criticizes the private self that can hide in both.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase means to turn the teaching wheel: to give teaching or set it in motion. Jifei Ruyi asks who will join him in turning it, while Huilin Zongben questions how it turns from within a mote of dust. Yinyuan Longqi records a patron’s request that teaching be given; a lamp record raises Manjusri’s request to the Buddha; the Zutang Ji narrator describes Jiashan Shanhui as already having taught publicly. Dahui Zonggao performs three staff strikes while declaring that the teaching wheel has turned three times.

Senses.Explanation: A turning word is a response demanded or supplied to pivot a case or stuck encounter. In the wild-fox case the old man asks Baizhang Huaihai to provide one in his place, and Baizhang's answer releases him. Wumen Huikai challenges readers to lay one down at the decisive point of a case. Yunmen Wenyan prizes Baling's three turning words as sufficient repayment of his teaching debt. Xuedou Chongxian asks each Chan guest to supply one to the broken-fan challenge. Baiyan Mingzhe asks an interlocutor for a different turning word that would accord with him. Tianyi Yihuai asks the community to provide one on Shakyamuni's behalf against the demon king. In a reported exchange Shun Bujue criticizes Sheng for winning a monastery with only one turning word while still not having dreamed of the teaching. The term therefore names a consequential pivoting response, not any clever sentence.

Senses.Note: The expression ranges from literal bodily motion to the ability to change direction in an encounter. Added nouns specify a road, place, or phrase for such a turn; they should not make every bare occurrence technical.

Occurrences.Kwic: 如何是轉身一路？汝行荒草裏，我又入深村。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J27/J27nB193.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yinyuan (隱元禪師語錄): Yinyuan Longqi utters the exact quoted wording in the complete source unit.

Senses.Explanation: To turn around is either the ordinary bodily action or, in an exchange, the ability to change direction and respond where one's present course is exhausted. The literal use remains visible when Mayu Baoche turns to sit and when Hanyue Fazang turns and walks away. The records also extend that motion into responsive freedom: Yuanwu Keqin says Zhaozhou has a place of free turning, Hongzhi Zhengjue requires a road of turning, and Feiyin Tongrong pairs turning with shifting one's step so one can remain alive in the thorn forest. The compounds make the extension explicit. Yuanwu calls speaking where there are no words and going where one cannot go a place to turn; an unnamed monk asks Poshan Haiming for a turning phrase; and the Baoning dialogue asks for a road of turning in the face of death. These uses share a change of direction, but the bare verb can still describe nothing more than physically turning around.

Senses.Explanation: A turning phrase is the utterance demanded when a position, distinction, or inherited answer must be turned rather than merely repeated; its adequacy is tested by what happens next in the exchange. Baoning Renyong asks how the turning phrase will be spoken thirty years later and answers after a pause. Tian'an Sheng asks for it when delusion and awakening are both forgotten; Sanshan Denglai places it between the intimate phrase and the phrase among other kinds. Mingjue Cong asks how to speak it after the road and home phrases, while Liao'an Qingyu sets it at the ten-thousand-fathom cliff. An anonymous old master says a direct presentation still lacks the turning phrase and then supplies a verse after asking the assembly.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J33/J33nB294.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Liangting Ting of Yunxi (雲溪俍亭挺禪師語錄): Langting Jingting rejects speech that merely rolls in the mouth because it was memorized from a book or guessed through conceptual activity.

Senses.Explanation: Rolling and turning freely is the records' kinetic appraisal for handling that responds without sticking, repeatedly pictured as a gourd rolling on water. Dahui Zonggao uses the water-gourd image for a person whose handling cannot be caught, constrained, entangled, drawn, or arranged. In discussing Nanyang Huizhong's exchange, he says the National Teacher turns without remaining in one corner and answers the question without failing it. Yuanwu Keqin describes sayings returning to oneself and turning toward the lively place, but he also contrasts natural rolling with deliberative calculation. Langting Jingting supplies the adverse control: phrases formed directly in season roll without effort, whereas words that merely roll in one's mouth after being memorized from a book have no connection. The praise therefore belongs to responsive handling, not verbal fluency or restless motion by itself.

Senses.Explanation: The snub-nosed snake enters the record as Xuefeng Yicun's own warning: on South Mountain there is a snub-nosed snake, and you had all best watch out. Changqing Huileng answered at once that many in the hall had just lost their lives, Xuansha Shibei asked what anyone wanted with South Mountain, and Yunmen Wenyan thrust his staff toward Xuefeng in feigned fear. Yuanwu Keqin set the demonstration in the Blue Cliff Record among the showings of Xuefeng, and Baiyun Shouduan versified it — the snake of Xianggu ridge lies across the high road, master Leng threw his life away, Yunmen handled it living, but better never to touch South Mountain at all. Gaofeng Yuanmiao raised the case to call Xuefeng a habitual thief whose sons botched the haul, and Shixi Xinyue said the Min elder is a bright mirror, yet once the snake enters the bamboo tube the crooked heart is still there. Jieshi Zhipeng ended a hall address by throwing down his staff — how does that compare with the South-Mountain snub-nosed snake? Xisou Shaotan flipped it: you would take it for the South-Mountain snub-nosed snake, but it is a Tiantai staff, worth not a cent. Wuyi Yuanlai set it beside a sparrow alive in a tiger's throat, Tian'an Sheng asked who the snake-handler is, and Tanfang Shouzhong threw the fire at a cremation — in the fire a snub-nosed snake-dragon, killers beyond count. The creature's earliest carrier is the Patriarchs' Hall Anthology of 952: inside its life of Xuefeng Yicun the warning stands with both disciples' substitute answers — Changqing Huileng's many in this hall have lost their lives, and Xuansha Shibei's what do you want with South Mountain — and with the earliest extant verses on the case, one of them naming Xuefeng as the snake's keeper who lodged it on South Mountain. Yuanwu Keqin's Blue Cliff Record commentary retells the demonstration while weighing Xuefeng's showing: a word from him was no workshop of cleverness but a thing that sits astride past and present and leaves no room for conjecture — and Leng the Elder answered from the assembly that the hall had just lost a houseful of lives. Later masters raised the old case and made it bear their own verdicts. Baiyun Shouduan headed a verse-comment entry with the warning line and versified its two answerers, Changqing Huileng and Yunmen Wenyan. Gaofeng Yuanmiao recited the case whole — the warning, Changqing Huileng's response, Yunmen Wenyan's fear-feint with the staff, Xuansha Shibei's verdict and his own what-do-you-want-with-South-Mountain — then delivered his own: Xuefeng was a habitual thief, but his sons were poor accomplices, and the botched haul has stunk for a thousand years. Shixi Xinyue, closing a retreat, called the Min elder a bright mirror that shows whatever comes — yet the snake has entered the bamboo tube and the crooked heart is still there — and he dared anyone to scratch an itch on a venomous snake's head. The masters also took the creature as their own stock figure. Jieshi Zhipeng closed a hall address with it — things are one family across ten thousand differences, Yunmen's paste-cake, Zhaozhou's tea, then the staff thrown down: how does that compare with the South-Mountain snub-nosed snake? Xisou Shaotan held out the one thing black as lacquer that goes in and out of the face-door and flipped it — you would take it for the South-Mountain snub-nosed snake, but it is a Tiantai staff, worth not a cent. Wuyi Yuanlai, at a lecture installation, set the rotted staff beside the snake and snapped it for the marvel, next to the sparrow rescued alive from a tiger's throat. Tian'an Sheng weighed Guizong's cut snake and Shushan's wooden snake against the South-Mountain creature — snake-handling needs a snake-handler's hand; who is it? — and flicked his staff: snake, snake. At a cremation in Tanfang Shouzhong's record the creature turned the funeral fire: after four lines on the great being finishing the sutra, Tanfang threw the torch — in the fire a snub-nosed snake-dragon, killers beyond count — and moved on to the next pyre.
